transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Cortez (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Harrowsmith), Jonas Reed (Harrowsmith), Priya Menon (Harrowsmith), Ethan Lowe (Harrowsmith)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Harrowsmith is evaluating Redwood Private for latency-sensitive inference. Primary concerns: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway, private endpoints (privatelink style), egress IPs and data-residency (EU workloads), SOC2/SSO/KMS integration, and ability to run a pilot in their staging account. SE to propose network diagram and mini-pilot cluster.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate your time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, this is Liam our Senior SE. Can we do quick intros?
[00:10] Nina: Nina Patel here, cloud architect for Harrowsmith. Jonas is our SRE, Priya handles security, Ethan does platform.
[00:18] Jonas: Yep, hi all.
[00:20] Liam: Cool. Quick agenda, want to understand current infra, traffic patterns, and constraints — region residency, egress, and how you'll want to connect, right?
[00:30] Nina: Correct. We're exploring private deployment. Our goal is to keep inference traffic inside AWS, no public internet hops, and meet EU data residency for certain customer segments.
[00:40] Priya: Security is number one; we need SOC2 docs, SAML SSO, KMS integration and audit logs retained for 1 year. Also RBAC for engineers.
[00:52] Maya: Absolutely, we'll share our security pack. Quick check — do you have a Transit Gateway already or primarily VPC peering?
[01:02] Jonas: We run a TGW in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 for a subset of services, but some teams still use direct peering. We prefer TGW for scale.
[01:12] Liam: Great, Redwood Private supports Transit Gateway attachments and also direct VPC peering and PrivateLink-style endpoints for private control-plane connectivity. Small note: our private endpoint is effectively a privatelink service that the customer can accept into their VPC.
[01:30] Ethan: What's the difference operationally? If we use TGW vs privatelink, any constraints?
[01:38] Liam: Good q. TGW is great for many-to-many connectivity, but you'll need route tables and attachment policies. PrivateLink / Private Endpoint gives you an interface endpoint with ENIs in your subnets — it avoids route table proliferation and keeps traffic localized. For egress, if you want all traffic to remain in-region we recommend endpoint + TGW with route controls.
[01:58] Nina: We have a hard requirement that EU customer data must not leave eu-west-1. Can Redwood pin model serving to that region?
[02:06] Maya: Yes, Private lets you pin model versions and serve in region. We'll need to confirm model availability in eu-west-1 for the model you pick; we can recommend close equivalents if not available.
[02:18] Priya: For keys, KMS integration is a must. We use AWS KMS and HSM for some secrets. Does Redwood Private support CMKs?
[02:26] Liam: We integrate with customer KMS using AWS key policies; we also support customer-managed HSM for private deployment in the on-prem package. There was a recent doc we can share that describes the workflow.
[02:38] Jonas: Awesome. On networking specifics — egress IPs. We have legacy allow-lists that expect static egress IPs. Can you provide those?
[02:46] Maya: Yes, we'll provide egress IP ranges for dedicated clusters. For Private, we usually give a set of NAT or egress ranges you can whitelist; if you're behind TGW we'll show how to SNAT through your NAT gateway.
[02:58] Ethan: What about KV cache / token passing — will the KV cache talk back to the control plane over public interface? We want everything private.
[03:06] Liam: The KV cache and model inference stays on the private dataplane in your VPC for Private deployments. The control plane can be run in a customer-managed private control-plane if needed; otherwise Redwood offers a private control-plane that establishes a mutual TLS channel over PrivateLink. There might be a mis-transcription here: sometimes the transcriber shows K V cash instead of KV cache.
[03:26] Nina: That last bit about private control-plane — we prefer fully customer-managed control plane if possible, for compliance. Is that an option?
[03:34] Maya: Yes, we offer a private control-plane package where the control plane is deployed into your account, or we can run a private control-plane in our VPC but connect via accepted PrivateLink endpoints. Both patterns are supported, trade-offs on ops ownership.
[03:48] Priya: For audits, we need admin activity logs and per-request tracing. Are logs accessible to us?
[03:56] Liam: You get API-level audit logs; for Private we can route logs to your CloudWatch / S3 using our delivery integration. We'll capture token-level cost/latency breakdowns as well.
[04:10] Jonas: Bandwidth — our inference traffic could be spiky, up to 600 Mbps sustained for certain inference shard sets. Any bandwidth limitations?
[04:18] Liam: Depends on instance sizing in the cluster. For Private, you control the instance types and NICs. We recommend up to 100 Gbps NICs for heavy throughput. We'll include a sizing guide.
[04:30] Maya: Quick question — timeline? Are you looking to pilot in staging soon?
[04:34] Nina: We'd like a pilot in staging within 2 weeks, but realistic earliest is the week of Aug 6 since we need internal approvals.
[04:42] Maya: Ok, target week of 2028-08-06 for a mini-pilot. We'll prepare a mini cluster template for your staging account.
[04:50] Ethan: Who will own the pilot infra setup? We prefer Redwood to provide CloudFormation/Terraform modules to speed this up.
[04:56] Liam: We'll provide Terraform modules and a runbook. We can also do a joint run to bootstrap.
[05:04] Priya: SLA speak — if we do Private, what uptime and support tiers are typical?
[05:10] Maya: For Dedicated/Private customers we offer SLA-backed uptime; specifics depend on commitment level. We'll include options and pricing in the follow-up.
[05:18] Jonas: Network-wise, do we need to modify route tables across all subnets? We have a mix of private and public subnets in our VPCs.
[05:26] Liam: For PrivateLink you need interface endpoints in private subnets where the platform components talk to. For TGW attachments you put routes in the transit route tables. We can draft an IP plan that minimizes changes to existing production route tables.
[05:40] Nina: We also have regulatory constraints — EU data must stay in eu-west-1 and we want no egress to US for those flows. Is cross-region replication an opt-in?
[05:50] Liam: Yes, cross-region replication is opt-in. You can pin workloads and avoid replication. If you enable multi-region for failover, then you'd configure which regions can receive replicas.
[06:02] Maya: On IAM and SSO — do you use SAML or OIDC?
[06:06] Priya: SAML SSO with Okta. We also require SCIM for provisioning.
[06:12] Liam: Redwood supports SAML and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll send the SSO integration guide — that's in the security pack link.
[06:20] Nina: Any hard limits on number of endpoints per account? We create a lot of interface ENIs for other services and worry about ENI quotas.
[06:28] Liam: Good point. Interface endpoints consume ENIs — we can provide a pattern that uses shared ENIs at scale and/or route via TGW to reduce ENI count. We'll include quota guidance.
[06:40] Jonas: Ok can you walk briefly through a recommended topology?
[06:44] Liam: Sure. Option A: TGW-centric — Redwood cluster in a dedicated VPC attached to your TGW, advertise routes, control egress via your NAT. Pros: one attachment, simple routing for many VPCs. Cons: route table governance. Option B: PrivateLink — Redwood publishes a service endpoint, you accept interface endpoint in each VPC/subnet. Pros: per-VPC granular control, no TGW changes. Cons: ENI quotas and more endpoints to manage. Option C: Hybrid — Control plane via PrivateLink, dataplane attached via TGW peering for high throughput.
[07:22] Nina: Hybrid sounds interesting. Can you do canary model rollouts across regions? We want to route EU users to EU-only models.
[07:30] Maya: Yes, our rollout policies let you route by region/customer segment and fallback to compatible models if needed. We'll need to set up routing policies in the control plane.
[07:40] Priya: During the pilot, we want to run some security tests — pen test and configuration review. Redwood okay with that?
[07:46] Maya: Yes, customers can run security tests under NDA; we'll coordinate scope.
[07:52] Nina: Regarding cost, if we run in Private and choose larger instances for throughput, what's the billing model? Fixed commit or usage?
[07:58] Maya: For Private it's typically platform fee + infra costs; Dedicated supports reserved capacity contracts for predictable throughput. We'll include pricing scenarios.
[08:08] Ethan: Do you have prebuilt Terraform modules for govcloud / specialized regions? We have internal forks for some restricted regions.
[08:14] Liam: We have modules for standard commercial regions; for GovCloud/air-gapped we have a slightly different deployment that might need manual steps. We'll flag that in the runbook.
[08:24] Jonas: Egress IPs again — will the egress IP change if we scale up nodes?
[08:30] Liam: If you NAT through your NAT gateway, egress is your IPs. If Redwood provides NAT egress, we give a stable pool per cluster, but we can also announce static ranges. We'll make sure you have stable allowlistable IPs for the pilot.
[08:46] Maya: Quick check — any blocks we haven't touched? Data retention?
[08:50] Priya: We need logs to be kept for 12 months and encrypted at rest with CMKs. Also need ability to export logs for audit.
[08:58] Liam: That's supported. We'll include the S3/CloudWatch export configuration in the docs.
[09:06] Nina: Do you support per-tenant encryption keys? We have customers that require customer-key per tenant.
[09:12] Liam: We can do per-tenant key scoping for secrets; for per-tenant model encryption we need to discuss specifics but generally yes, via CMKs and key policies.
[09:24] Ethan: For troubleshooting, we need packet-level visibility sometimes. Any support for VPC flow logs or mirror sessions?
[09:32] Liam: You can enable VPC flow logs and we surface relevant traces. For packet mirror sessions it's possible but typically only for deep forensic work — we can coordinate that.
[09:44] Jonas: Ok, so immediate asks: security pack, egress ranges, Terraform modules, sample network diagram and a pilot template.
[09:52] Maya: We'll deliver those. We'll also want to do a network diagram review session — propose Tue 2028-08-01 16:00 UTC?
[09:58] Nina: That works for us except a few on the team. We'll confirm.
[10:02] Priya: For the pilot we need the scope of what will be tested: functional inference, latency, failover, security posture.
[10:10] Maya: Agreed. We'll propose a test plan in the follow-up doc.
[10:16] Ethan: Any gotchas re: NAT gateway costs if we route egress through our NAT? We run into charges at scale.
[10:22] Liam: You'll incur NAT bandwidth costs. If you want to avoid double egress, we can show patterns to keep traffic within VPC and use direct peering so you pay once for the cloud provider egress. We'll provide cost guidance.
[10:36] Nina: One last: who will be our primary contact for the pilot setup?
[10:40] Maya: Primary will be me for procurement and Liam for technical.
[10:44] Jonas: Great.
[10:46] Maya: Ok wrapping up — recap and next steps. We'll share security pack + SOC2 summary, SSO integration guide, egress IP list, Terraform modules, and a proposed network topology doc. We'll aim to have these to you by 2028-08-02. Pilot kickoff targeted week of 2028-08-06, and we'll set a follow-up network diagram session for 2028-08-01.
[11:12] Nina: Sounds good. We'll send our VPC CIDRs and TGW attachments by 2028-08-03.
[11:18] Priya: We'll prep compliance questions in advance.
[11:22] Maya: Perfect. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the pack and a calendar invite for the diagram review.
[11:28] Jonas: Thanks, bye.
